newsitem.title: UK: High European gas oil prices open U.S. arbitrage.
newsitem.headline: High European gas oil prices open U.S. arbitrage.

text.p: High gas oil prices in Europe -- especially low sulphur diesel -- have opened the arbitrage door from North America wide open, but traders said the move was a high-risk gamble while prices were so volatile.
At least three cargoes of Canadian gas oil were headed for the Mediterranean and on Tuesday shipbrokers reported 42,000 tonnes sailing from the U.S. Gulf to Northern Europe loading September 14.
"Given the sheer numbers in Europe I wouldn't be surprised to see some cargoes coming over," one trader said.

Low sulphur was worth 67.25 cents per gallon fob New York on Tuesday morning, equivalent to $211.50 a tonne, versus cif Europe prices of $228, leaving ample margin to ship the product from one centre to the other.
Shipbrokers say transatlantic freight costs stand at $11 per tonne on a 40,000 tonne vessel.
But many remain cautious about arbitrage opportunities while the benchmark IPE futures market was so volatile.
"We were looking at the possibility of bringing 0.05 percent from the U.S. Gulf, but we decided it was too risky at the moment while the market is so jumpy," one trader said.

Dealers also noted that the amount of gas oil making the journey would be limited because of a quality mismatch between the U.S. and Europe -- the minimum cetane number in the United States is 40 while in Europe it is 49.
"It is possible to find the right spec, there's just not that much. We've found parcels in the past," one trader said.
"Not all U.S. diesel would meet the European specification, but a fair amount would. After about four cargoes (sold) there would probably be a shortage," one trader said.

The arbitrage coincides with inflated premiums on low sulphur diesel ahead of the introduction of European Union 0.05 percent sulphur regulations on October 1, but traders said it was too early to say whether U.S. gas oil would become a regular feature in the European spot market. "It remains to be seen what the low sulphur premiums do when the rules come into force. I don't expect it will become a regular route although arb opportunities like this may become a little more frequent," one trader said.
